One who is to come"?
In the time of John the Baptist and Jesus the question was
a very living one and the hearts of the Jewish people were
aglow with hope in the One who was to come. We refer to
the nation's hope in the Messiah, the King who was to reign
in the latter days of blessedness, who was to bring to an end
all sorrow and wrong on the earth and to set up the kingdom
of God, a kingdom of righteousness and salvation. Such
hopes arose from the words of the ancient prophets, which
were carefully preserved in the Scriptures and cherished
with yearning hearts. And from hopes of this kind arose the
question: When will the expected Messiah come? Who will
it be? "Watchman, what of the night?" And it is from the
ferment of such hopes that Jesus is challenged with the
question: "Are you He?"
The question flows from the Messianic hope. Hence we
ourselves can ask such a question only if such a hope is alive
in us. It is a question which has no meaning for all those who
are satisfied with the world as it is. Whether it be that the
world is for them a place of pleasure and enjoyment, where
they disregard the shadows which of course there are in life,
and cling to the light that is given them, banishing cares
from their minds and seizing the joys which each day brings.
Or again it might be that the world for such people is a
sphere in which they fulfil a vocation to work and struggle,
accomplishing their tasks either as individuals or com-
munities, tasks which reward initiative and self-sacrifice, and
make life worth living.
"For the strong man the world is not silent and un-
responsive. Why should such a one waste his life in dreaming
of eternity? What he knows can be grasped and embodied!"
It cannot be denied that men to-day are to a large extent
satisfied with the world and that, in so far as they are not,
they live in the belief that it lies in their own hands to give
the world the form which they consider right, and that for
this high aim they are prepared to sacrifice their time and
strength and in fact also their property and blood. But
